title: Fiction book writing
prompt: I want to write a novel
summary: A novel is a long invented story in prose, built to keep a reader turning pages. Writers think in layers: a premise with real stakes, characters who want things, a plot of scenes that turn on cause and effect, and narration and prose that control what the reader knows and feels. Under all of it sits the reader’s experience: questions opened, answers delayed, promises kept. Most of the work is a loop: plan, draft fast, then revise against how real readers respond. Structure models and rules of thumb are tools for diagnosing a draft, not forms to fill in.

nodes.plain: A long invented story told in prose. SFWA’s award rules count 40,000 words or more as a novel.
nodes.ask: What will the reader feel on the last page, and what keeps them turning pages to get there?
nodes.trouble: Readers stop halfway, or finish and feel nothing.

nodes.plain: The core situation: a character in a setting with a problem. It often starts as a what-if question.
nodes.does: Gives every later choice a test: does this serve the premise?
nodes.ask: Who is in trouble, where, and why can she not walk away?
nodes.trouble: You cannot say what the book is about without listing events.

nodes.does: Tests the premise: if it will not fit in one line, the story is not clear yet.
nodes.ask: Who has the most to lose, and what do they want to win?
nodes.trouble: You need names, subplots or “and then” to explain the book.

nodes.plain: Every promise the story makes, it must keep. Chekhov: do not put a loaded gun on stage unless someone will fire it.
nodes.does: Builds trust: readers learn that details matter, so they read closely.
nodes.ask: What did page one promise, and where do I pay it off?
nodes.trouble: Readers feel cheated: a setup goes nowhere, or the ending comes from nowhere.

feel.why: A promise goes out and travels round; the payoff brings it home and closes the circle.

sources.label: Brandon Sanderson, “2025 Guide to Plot (Lecture #2)”
sources.page: The Plot Framework: Promise, Progress, and Payoff

sources.label: Anton Chekhov, Letter to A. S. Lazarev-Gruzinsky

nodes.plain: The question the story raises early and answers late. Here: will Maya prove who wrote the list before 06:00?
nodes.does: Pulls the reader to the end: they keep reading to get the answer.
nodes.ask: What question does chapter one plant, and where exactly is it answered?
nodes.trouble: Readers drift away in the middle: the question was answered too soon, or never asked.

feel.why: An open question itches: sharp enough to nag, light enough to hang in the air until the end.

sources.label: Lee Child, “A Simple Way to Create Suspense”
Story Grid, “The Five Commandments of Storytelling”

nodes.plain: What the character loses if she fails. Bell groups stakes as three kinds of death: physical, professional and psychological.
nodes.does: Sets how much the reader cares about each conflict.
nodes.ask: What happens if she fails, and how could it get worse?
nodes.range: Personal and public stakes (Maass); at least one kind of death (Bell)
nodes.trouble: Big explosions but a bored reader: the loss is not personal.

nodes.plain: The people who do things in the story: a protagonist, an opponent and the cast around them.
nodes.does: Make events matter: readers care because things happen to someone.
nodes.ask: Who wants what, and how do they get in each other’s way?
nodes.trouble: Characters act only because the plot needs them to.

nodes.plain: The character whose goal drives the story. Truby: one specific desire line runs through the whole book.
nodes.does: Gives the reader someone to follow, and a goal to measure progress against.
nodes.ask: What does she want, and how will we know if she gets it?
nodes.trouble: She reacts but never chooses; things just happen to her.

nodes.plain: The want is the outer goal she chases. The need is the truth that frees her from a lie she believes, often since an old wound.
nodes.does: Gives the arc a direction: the plot pushes her to choose the need over the want.
nodes.ask: What lie does she believe, and what old wound made her believe it?
nodes.trouble: The plot problem is solved, but she is the same person she was on page one.

feel.why: Two goals pull against each other inside one person, so the body never quite settles.

nodes.plain: Sanderson’s three dials for a character: how likable, how proactive and how competent they are.
nodes.does: Let you tune how readers feel about a character without changing the plot.
nodes.ask: Which slider is low, and is that on purpose?
nodes.range: Each slider low to high; a character can move up or down during the story
nodes.trouble: A character feels flat or annoying and you cannot say why.

nodes.plain: How the text shows who someone is. Burroway’s direct methods are appearance, speech, action and thought; authorial interpretation is the indirect one.
nodes.does: Lets readers build the person from evidence, so the person feels real.
nodes.ask: What does she do, say or notice that only she would?
nodes.trouble: The narrator says she is brave, but she never does anything brave.

nodes.does: Creates the conflict and sets how hard the protagonist must push.
nodes.ask: Why does he think he is right?
nodes.trouble: He is evil for no reason, or too weak to be a threat.

nodes.plain: How a character changes, or refuses to change, between the first page and the last. Weiland names five main arcs.
nodes.does: Gives the plot an inner meaning: events become the cause of change.
nodes.ask: Who is she at the end that she could not be at the start?
nodes.trouble: The climax would play out the same with the character from chapter one.

feel.why: A slow climb out of a lie toward the truth: warm, rounded and rising.

items.name: Positive change
items.plain: Believes a lie, overcomes it, and the new truth sets her free. Maya learns that speaking up is safer than silence.

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance

items.name: Flat
items.plain: Already believes the truth and holds on to it; she uses it to change the world around her.

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance

items.name: Disillusionment
items.plain: Overcomes the lie, but the truth she finds is tragic.

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs

items.name: Fall
items.plain: Clings to the lie, rejects the truth and ends up believing a worse lie.

sources.label: K.M. Weiland, Learn 5 Types of Character Arc at a Glance: The 3 Negative Arcs

items.name: Corruption
items.plain: Sees the truth, rejects it, and embraces the lie to get what she wants.

nodes.plain: The cast as a network. Truby compares every character with the hero and with each other, so the differences become clear.
nodes.does: Makes each character sharper, because the others show what they are not.
nodes.ask: How does each character push on the hero?
nodes.trouble: Two characters do the same job; you could merge them.

nodes.plain: The events and the order you show them in. Forster: a story asks “and then?”, a plot asks “why?”.
nodes.does: Controls what the reader learns when, so tension builds toward the climax.
nodes.ask: Does each event cause the next one?
nodes.trouble: A saggy middle: events follow “and then” instead of “therefore” or “but”.

nodes.plain: Four kinds of story thread: milieu, inquiry, character and event. Each opens and closes, and threads nest like Russian dolls.
nodes.does: Tells you how each thread must end, and that inner threads close before outer ones.
nodes.ask: Which thread did I open first, and does the ending close it?
nodes.trouble: The ending answers the wrong question, so the book feels unfinished.

nodes.does: Gives the plot its shape: the reader feels it change gear at each turn.
nodes.ask: What turns here, and what can she no longer do?
nodes.trouble: Things happen, but nothing changes the direction of the story.

nodes.does: Starts the story’s engine and raises the dramatic question.
nodes.ask: What breaks the normal world, and can she ignore it?
nodes.range: About 10% (Brody) to 12% (Weiland) of the way through
nodes.trouble: Chapters of backstory before anything happens.

nodes.plain: The protagonist’s active answer to the story’s last crisis. It shows who she really is under pressure.
nodes.does: Answers the dramatic question and pays off the main promises.
nodes.ask: Does she win or lose because of a choice she makes?
nodes.range: Starts about 90% of the way through (Weiland)
nodes.trouble: Luck, or another character, solves the problem for her.

nodes.plain: The character tries to solve a problem and fails; the failure creates the next problem. Two variants: “yes, but” and “no, and”.
nodes.does: Drives the middle of the book: each failure raises the stakes for the next try.
nodes.ask: How does this failure make things worse?
nodes.trouble: Each problem is solved cleanly, so the middle sags.

nodes.plain: The rise and fall of fortune across a story. A study of 1,327 Project Gutenberg stories found six basic shapes.
nodes.does: Lets you see the whole book’s emotional curve at once and choose where it turns.
nodes.ask: Where is the lowest point, and where does fortune turn?
nodes.trouble: The line stays flat: nothing gets much better or much worse.

nodes.does: Moves the story one step at a time, in front of the reader.
nodes.ask: What changes between the start and the end of this scene?
nodes.trouble: Scenes of people talking in which nothing turns.

nodes.plain: Ingermanson’s two-part rhythm. A scene runs goal, conflict, disaster; a sequel runs reaction, dilemma, decision, and the decision sets the next goal.
nodes.does: Alternates action and recovery, so each scene feeds the next.
nodes.ask: What is her goal at the start of this scene, and what does she decide at the end of the sequel?
nodes.trouble: Scenes stop with no consequence, or the character never pauses to react.

nodes.plain: What the viewpoint character wants in this scene. It must be specific and clear: get the list to security.
nodes.does: Gives the scene a direction and a test of success.
nodes.ask: What exactly does she want in the next ten pages?
nodes.trouble: A vague wish, such as “she wants to feel safe”.

nodes.plain: The obstacles between the character and her goal. Voss’s guard blocks the stairs.
nodes.does: Makes the reader doubt the outcome.
nodes.ask: What stands in her way, and does it get harder?
nodes.trouble: She reaches her goal without a fight.
nodes.deeper: Motivation-reaction units: the beat-by-beat pattern inside a scene, as Ingermanson teaches it.

nodes.plain: She fails to reach the goal, or wins and makes things worse. Security is in on it.
nodes.does: Keeps tension high. Ingermanson warns that simply granting the goal ends the tension.
nodes.ask: How does this scene end worse than it began?
nodes.trouble: Scenes end with the problem solved and nothing to pull the reader on.

nodes.plain: Her emotional follow-through after the disaster. Panic: she hides and shakes.
nodes.does: Lets the reader feel the blow and catch their breath.
nodes.ask: How does the disaster hit her?
nodes.trouble: Nothing seems to affect her.

nodes.plain: A situation with no good options. Run home, or stay and warn bed four?
nodes.does: Shows her values through what she must give up.
nodes.ask: What will each option cost her?
nodes.trouble: The right choice is obvious, so there is no suspense.

nodes.plain: She chooses what to do. The decision makes her proactive again and sets the next goal: she stays.
nodes.does: Restarts the cycle with a new scene goal.
nodes.ask: What will she do now?
nodes.trouble: Things happen to her; she never decides.

nodes.plain: The change in a value-charged condition, such as safe to hunted, between the start and the end of a scene. McKee calls a scene that does not turn a nonevent.
nodes.does: Checks that each scene earns its place.
nodes.ask: What value is at stake, and is it plus or minus at each end of the scene?
nodes.range: Plus to minus, or minus to plus; the same charge at both ends means no turn
nodes.trouble: A scene starts and ends in the same place.

nodes.does: Give you a checklist to diagnose a draft: what is missing, early or late.
nodes.ask: Which model fits my genre, and where do my turns fall on it?
nodes.trouble: A formula followed beat by beat; the story feels mechanical.

items.name: Seven-point structure
items.plain: Wells: hook, plot turn 1, pinch 1, midpoint, pinch 2, plot turn 2, resolution. Plan backward from the resolution.

nodes.plain: Smaller stories woven round the main plot. In Save the Cat the B story starts near 22% and brings in people who help the hero learn the theme.
nodes.does: Adds depth and lets the middle breathe without stopping the main plot.
nodes.ask: How does this subplot bear on the main question or the theme?
nodes.trouble: You could cut a subplot and nothing in the main plot would change.

sources.label: Jessica Brody, Save the Cat! Writes a Novel Starter Kit

nodes.plain: Each event happens because of the one before. Parker and Stone: join beats with “therefore” or “but”, never “and then”.
nodes.does: Makes events feel surprising and inevitable at the same time.
nodes.ask: Can I join these scenes with “therefore” or “but” instead of “and then”?
nodes.trouble: Scenes could swap places and nothing would change.

nodes.plain: Where and when the story happens. It is more than a backdrop: it sets the mood and can work with or against the characters.
nodes.does: Grounds the story in a concrete world and puts pressure on the characters.
nodes.ask: How does this place make her problem worse?
nodes.trouble: Characters talk in a white room; the story could happen anywhere.

nodes.plain: The physical place and the moment in time. Here: St Jude’s hospital in Boston, 2 a.m. on a snowy January night.
nodes.does: Limits what is possible and gives the senses something to work with.
nodes.ask: Why must this story happen here, and now?
nodes.trouble: The reader cannot tell where the characters are or what time it is.

nodes.plain: The limits of how the story world works, from magic to hospital security. Sanderson’s second law: “Limitations > Powers”.
nodes.does: Lets the reader predict what is possible, so solutions feel earned.
nodes.ask: Does the reader understand this rule before it solves a problem?
nodes.trouble: A new power or rule appears just in time to save the hero.

nodes.plain: How the reader learns background facts. Jo Walton’s “incluing” scatters small pieces through the text instead of one info-dump.
nodes.does: Gives the reader what they need to understand, without stopping the story.
nodes.ask: Does the reader need this now, and can they pick it up from action?
nodes.trouble: Pages of history before the story starts, or characters telling each other what they both know.

nodes.plain: Who tells the story and from where. Burroway puts it as three questions: who speaks, who sees, and how much they know.
nodes.does: Controls what the reader can know and how close they feel to the characters.
nodes.ask: Whose eyes, and how close to them?
nodes.trouble: The reader is unsure whose head they are in.

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

nodes.plain: Whether the narration says “she ran” or “she runs”. Le Guin notes that both are made up: fictional past tense is not really past.
nodes.does: Sets how time feels: past tense can range across time, present tense keeps the reader in the moment.
nodes.ask: Do I need to move freely in time, or hold the reader in the moment?
nodes.trouble: The tense slips between paragraphs by accident.

items.name: Past
items.plain: “Maya ran.” Gives range: looking back, summary, and easy moves between earlier and later events.

sources.label: Myfanwy Collins, quoting Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft
Philip Pullman, Philip Pullman Calls Time on the Present Tense

items.name: Present
items.plain: “Maya runs.” Immediate, but Pullman argues that for a whole book it narrows what the prose can do.

nodes.plain: The personality you hear in the narration: word choice, rhythm, attitude and how much the narrator comments. It is not the same as the author’s own voice.
nodes.does: Colours every line: the same event reads differently in a different voice.
nodes.ask: If I hid the name, would you know this narrator?
nodes.trouble: The prose is correct but could be anyone’s.

feel.why: Voice is a texture: a grain you hear in every line, like the timbre of a person’s speech.

sources.label: OpenStax, Writing Guide

nodes.plain: The grammar of the narrator: I, you, or she. Third person splits further by how much the narrator can know.
nodes.does: Sets the reader’s access: one mind, or many.
nodes.ask: Who tells this story, and why that person?
nodes.trouble: The narrator knows things they could not know.

items.plain: “I”. A character tells the story, from the centre of the action or from the side.

items.name: Second person
items.plain: “You”. Rare and intimate, but it tells readers what they do and feel.

nodes.plain: How close the reader stands to a character’s mind. Gardner gives five steps, from a wide historical view to raw sensation.
nodes.does: Controls intimacy: close for strong feeling, far for overview and speed.
nodes.ask: How close should we be right now, and why change?
nodes.trouble: Sudden jumps in distance jar the reader.

nodes.plain: The character whose senses and thoughts the reader shares in a scene. Switching heads inside a scene is called head-hopping.
nodes.does: Decides what the reader can see, know and feel in each scene.
nodes.ask: Whose head gives this scene the most pressure?
nodes.trouble: Head-hopping: the reader is unsure whose thoughts they are reading.

nodes.plain: The actual words and sentences. Lee Child says good prose “trips forward”: each line pulls the reader into the next.
nodes.does: Turns the plan into an experience, line by line.
nodes.ask: Does each sentence earn its place and pull toward the next?
nodes.trouble: Readers skim; descriptions blur together.

nodes.plain: A concrete detail appeals to the senses. Burroway: it becomes significant when it also suggests an idea or a judgement.
nodes.does: Lets readers infer the meaning themselves, so it sticks.
nodes.ask: What one detail shows what this room, or this person, is really like?
nodes.trouble: Lists of generic details: “a nice room with a table and chairs”.

nodes.plain: Scene shows events moment by moment; summary tells them in compressed form. Burroway treats both as ways to manage time.
nodes.does: Sets the speed of the story: scene slows it down, summary moves fast.
nodes.ask: Does this moment deserve a scene, or one line of summary?
nodes.trouble: Big moments are summarised and small ones are dramatised.

items.name: Show (scene)
items.plain: Moment by moment, with action, dialogue and reaction. Immediate and dramatic.

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

items.name: Tell (summary)
items.plain: Compresses time. Useful for background, routine and repeated events, and for moving fast.

nodes.plain: What characters say to each other. Burroway: good dialogue reveals character, gives information, creates conflict and moves the story on.
nodes.does: Becomes action when the conversation can change something.
nodes.ask: What does each speaker want from this exchange?
nodes.trouble: Characters tell each other things they both already know.

nodes.plain: The words that show who is speaking. Leonard’s rules: never use a verb other than “said”, and never add an adverb to it.
nodes.does: Keep the reader oriented without drawing attention to themselves.
nodes.ask: Would the reader know who spoke without this tag?
nodes.trouble: He hissed menacingly; she exclaimed brightly.

items.name: “said”
items.plain: Neutral and almost invisible. Its only job is to name the speaker.

items.name: Action beat
items.plain: A small action names the speaker and adds meaning: He smiled. “Go home.”

nodes.plain: The pattern of long and short sentences. Provost shows that sentences of the same length become monotonous.
nodes.does: Keeps prose alive to the ear and steers the reader’s speed.
nodes.ask: Read it aloud: where does it drone?
nodes.range: A mix of short, medium and long sentences
nodes.trouble: Every sentence has the same length and shape.

nodes.plain: What the story is about beneath the events. Burroway: it grows out of setting, action, thought and repeated details, not out of a stated moral.
nodes.does: Ties the parts together and gives the ending its meaning.
nodes.ask: What does the ending say about how to live?
nodes.trouble: A message preached in dialogue, or an ending that contradicts the rest.

feel.why: Theme sits deep and still under the plot; you feel its weight more than you see it.

sources.label: Janet Burroway, Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft, 3e

nodes.plain: McKee’s one-sentence theme: the final value plus its cause. Here: justice wins because one person stops keeping quiet.
nodes.does: Tells you which scenes belong: each one argues for or against it.
nodes.ask: What value wins at the end, and what causes it?
nodes.trouble: The climax proves something different from what the book set out to explore.

feel.why: One clear claim, cut sharp and heavy enough to hold the book down.

sources.label: How Writers Read, Controlling Value

nodes.plain: A recurring image, object, word or sound that gains meaning by repetition. Here: the ward lights flicker, go dark, then burn steady.
nodes.does: Carries the theme without stating it.
nodes.ask: What image keeps coming back, and does it change?
nodes.trouble: A symbol appears once and is never used again.

nodes.plain: The feeling of living inside the story. Gardner calls good fiction a “vivid and continuous dream”.
nodes.does: Lets the story work on the reader without them noticing the words.
nodes.ask: What could wake the reader from the dream here?
nodes.trouble: Head-hopping, confusing exposition or a jarring word pulls the reader out.

feel.why: A vivid, continuous dream: soft, smooth and easy to sink into.

sources.label: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction
Susan DeFreitas, How Big of a Problem Is “Head Hopping”?

nodes.plain: Lee Child’s method: ask a question, then delay the answer. He uses it for the whole book, each chapter, each page and each sentence.
nodes.does: Keeps the reader reading at every scale.
nodes.ask: Which question is open right now?
nodes.trouble: All the questions are answered at once, and the reader stops.

sources.label: Lee Child, Writing Popular Fiction

sources.page: interview exchange on questions and answers

nodes.plain: Lines that pull the reader on. Lee Child: a first line makes a promise, and a good chapter ending satisfies without satiating.
nodes.does: Carries the reader across the gaps between chapters and sittings.
nodes.ask: Why would someone read the next page right now?
nodes.trouble: Chapters end at natural rest points, so readers rest.

nodes.does: Alternates pressure and recovery, so the next peak can rise again.
nodes.ask: Where does the reader get to breathe?
nodes.trouble: Non-stop action that numbs, or long calm stretches that lose the reader.

nodes.plain: The gap between what the reader knows and what the characters know. Hitchcock: show the bomb under the table and you get suspense, not just a short surprise.
nodes.does: Creates the reader’s main feelings: curiosity, worry and surprise.
nodes.ask: Who knows what, right now?
nodes.trouble: The reader always knows exactly what the characters know.

nodes.plain: The work from idea to finished book. MIT’s writing guide names four stages: prewriting, drafting, revising and editing.
nodes.does: Turns an idea into a book through repeated passes, each with a different aim.
nodes.ask: Which stage am I in, and am I doing the right kind of work for it?
nodes.trouble: Polishing chapter one forever; the draft never gets finished.

nodes.plain: Deciding what happens before you draft. George R. R. Martin splits writers into architects, who plan, and gardeners, who discover the story as they write.
nodes.does: Cuts dead ends from the draft or, for gardeners, gives just enough seed to start.
nodes.ask: How much must I know before I start?
nodes.trouble: Endless world-building and no draft, or a draft that stalls with nowhere to go.

nodes.plain: The plan of scenes in order, often on index cards. Scrivener’s corkboard shows each scene as a card you can move.
nodes.does: Lets you see and rearrange the whole story before or during drafting.
nodes.ask: Does each card cause the next one?
nodes.trouble: Cards full of events but no change, and gaps where the middle should be.

nodes.plain: Writing the story from start to end without stopping to perfect it. King: write with the door closed, rewrite with the door open.
nodes.does: Produces the raw material; you cannot revise a blank page.
nodes.ask: Am I writing forward, or rewriting chapter one again?
nodes.trouble: Stopping to edit each page and never reaching the end.

nodes.plain: The first complete version of the story. Anne Lamott: all good writers write bad first drafts.
nodes.does: Shows what the story is really about, so you can fix it.
nodes.ask: Is it finished, start to end, even if it is bad?
nodes.trouble: Treating the first draft as the book.

nodes.plain: How many words you write each day. Known paces run from Hemingway’s few hundred words to Trollope’s 250 words every quarter of an hour.
nodes.does: Sets how long the draft takes: 90,000 words at 1,000 a day is three months.
nodes.ask: What pace can I keep every day for months?
nodes.trouble: A big target that you miss, then give up.

items.name: 2,500 a day
items.plain: Trollope trained himself to write 250 words every quarter of an hour, so 2,500 words took about two and a half hours.

nodes.does: Decides the money, control and reach of the finished book.

nodes.trouble: Paying for a contract with no clear way to readers.

nodes.does: Lets professionals read and estimate the book without distraction.
nodes.ask: Does it follow the format this agent or publisher asks for?
nodes.trouble: Fancy fonts, single spacing, or no contact details.

nodes.plain: Read the draft as a reader, test it on others, rewrite, and repeat. King: the first draft is written with the door closed; revision opens it.
nodes.does: Turns a draft into a book, one round at a time.
nodes.ask: What is the biggest problem in this draft?
nodes.trouble: Fixing commas while the plot is broken.

sources.label: Stephen King, On Writing

nodes.plain: An outline made after drafting: one line per part for its main point. Gaps, repeats and weak order show up at once.
nodes.does: Makes the draft’s real structure visible.
nodes.ask: What does each chapter change?
nodes.trouble: Chapters where nothing changes, or the same beat twice.

nodes.plain: A full pass through the draft to fix one kind of problem. King’s rule of thumb: 2nd draft = 1st draft − 10%.
nodes.does: Cuts what does not serve the story and strengthens what does.
nodes.ask: What can I cut without losing anything?
nodes.trouble: The draft gets longer with every pass.

nodes.plain: The draft after a revision pass: leaner, and closer to the story you meant to tell.
nodes.does: Feeds the next round of revision, or goes on to editing.
nodes.ask: Is it ready for an editor, or does it need another round?
nodes.trouble: The problems readers flagged are still there.

nodes.plain: Something placed early is used later. The early placement creates an expectation; the later use fulfils it in a way that still surprises.
nodes.ask: What did I set up, and where does it pay off?

feel.why: Something sent out early travels round and comes back to close the loop.

sources.label: Anton Chekhov, Letter to A. S. Lazarev-Gruzinsky
Brandon Sanderson, “2025 Guide to Plot (Lecture #2)”
sources.page: The Plot Framework: Promise, Progress, and Payoff

nodes.plain: A loop in which each change pushes further in the same direction, so it speeds up.
nodes.ask: What feeds itself here, and what will stop it?

feel.why: Each turn feeds the next, so it climbs faster and faster.

sources.label: UK Government Office for Science, “An introductory systems thinking toolkit for civil servants”

nodes.plain: A loop that opposes change and pulls the system back toward a level.
nodes.ask: What pushes back here, and toward what level?

feel.why: Each push meets a counter-push, so it sinks back to rest.

sources.label: UK Government Office for Science, “An introductory systems thinking toolkit for civil servants”

nodes.plain: Parts that depend on each other, directly or indirectly, so a change in one changes the rest.
nodes.ask: If I remove this part, what else changes?

feel.why: Many small bodies circle and lean on each other; move one and the rest shift.

sources.label: National Geographic Education, Ecosystem
John Truby, Blockbuster User’s Manual

nodes.plain: Small units sit inside bigger units of the same kind, like beats in scenes and scenes in acts. Each unit follows the same rules.
nodes.ask: Does this unit open and close like the one around it?

feel.why: Shells inside shells: each one opens and closes round the next.

sources.label: Story Grid, “Units of Story: Beats, Tropes, Scenes, Sequences, and Quadrants”
sources.page: What are Units of Story?; Beats–Quadrants

nodes.plain: Plan a change, do it, study the result, then act on what you learned. Repeat.
nodes.ask: What did the last round teach me?

feel.why: A wheel that turns again and again, a little better each time.

sources.label: The W. Edwards Deming Institute, PDSA Cycle

assembly.title: Find the premise
assembly.text: Start with a what-if. Pin it down in one sentence, name the question the ending must answer, and decide what failure would cost.

assembly.title: Plan the story
assembly.text: Grow the premise into people, a place and a chain of events. Put the scenes on cards and arrange them, as much or as little as suits you.

assembly.title: Draft
assembly.text: Choose who tells the story and how close we stand, then write it through to the end at a steady daily pace. Do not stop to polish.

assembly.title: Revise
assembly.text: Read the draft as a reader, test it on beta readers, find the theme you actually wrote, and cut it to length. Repeat until the big problems are gone.

assembly.title: Edit
assembly.text: Edit from big to small: structure, then sentences, then consistency, then typos. Format the result as a standard manuscript.

assembly.title: Publish
assembly.text: Choose a path to readers. The manuscript becomes a paperback, a hardback, an e-book or an audiobook.
